summary:
We are "NEXUS BETHA", the senior group from the Gimnasio Campestre Los Cerezos School. The challenge we chose was the “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer,” in which we developed a game in Scratch by the method block by block named "NEXUS BASE GAME". In the game the player plays as an astronaut that lives at a base on the Moon South Pole. 
The purpose of this game is for children ages 7–12 learn in an interesting, easy, attractive, funny, real and physically accurate way how to manage and ration a base’s energy to keep it running effectively, allocating it among life support, radiation protection, transportation, living modules, and solar panels and investigation in the Moon. All of this is intended to address the issue of the difficulties children face when learning about physical and spatial concepts, due to rigid and/or boring teaching methods that hinder their learning.
details:
NEXUS BETHA (Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer Challenge)

We are NEXUS BETHA, the senior team from Gimnasio Campestre Los Cerezos School. For this challenge, we chose “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer”, developing an interactive educational game named "NEXUS BASE GAME" using Scratch, programmed y the method block by block.

Our project takes players on an exciting journey to the Moon's South Pole, where they take on the role of an astronaut responsible for managing and maintaining a lunar base. Their main mission is to ensure the base continues operating successfully by making strategic decisions about how to distribute its limited energy resources.

The game focuses on energy management and introduces players to the different systems that make a lunar settlement possible, including life support, radiation protection, transportation, living modules, solar panels, and scientific research. Players must decide how much energy to allocate to each system, understanding that prioritizing one activity may limit the resources available for another. This creates realistic engineering trade-offs, showing that every decision has consequences and that resources in space cannot be used without careful planning.

The main benefit of our project is that it transforms complex scientific and engineering concepts into an accessible, interactive, and entertaining experience. Designed specifically for children ages 7–12, the game uses simple explanations, engaging visuals, and gameplay mechanics to make learning easier and more enjoyable. We want children to undertand space and physic factor in a dynamic way that makes them want to learn instead of simply presenting facts about space exploration.

Our intended impact is to encourage curiosity about space, develop problem-solving and critical-thinking skills, and introduce younger generations to the importance of engineering and scientific decision-making. We also aim to demonstrate that learning about physics and space does not have to be limited to traditional teaching methods: it can become an exciting experience in which children learn by experimenting, making decisions, and observing their consequences.

For development, we used Scratch, a visual programming platform that allows users to create interactive projects through a block-based coding system. We built our game block by block, organizing its mechanics, interactions, and gameplay elements to create a functional prototype. This approach allowed us to turn our initial concept into an accessible digital experience without requiring advanced programming languages or specialized hardware and with an easy management for children 7-12 years to use the game and understand it.

What makes our project creative and different from the others is the combination of space exploration, resource management, and interactive learning. Rather than creating another educational presentation about the Moon, we designed a simulation in which children become active participants in a lunar mission. But also, we used only real and verificated data from the NASA's and ESA's investigations, we aimed to develope a game that was not only about entretainment, but of representation of how a real Moon Base would wotk. We don't want the players just to be simply told of how a lunar base works; we want the to take decisions that may affect its operation and survival.

When developing and investigating, our team considered several important factors:

  • Age: Making the game understandable, engaging, and enjoyable for children ages 7–12.
  • Scientific accuracy: Keeping the mechanics grounded in real challenges associated with lunar exploration and energy management (We used ONLY NASA and ESA resources for our infomration, in order to make in real and physically accurate).
  • Educational value: Ensuring that every gameplay mechanic teaches a meaningful scientific or engineering concept.
  • Resource limitations: Representing the reality that energy is limited and must be distributed strategically.
  • User engagement: Incorporating an appealing space environment and interactive challenges to maintain players' interest (Focused especifically into catching the attention form children 7-12 years old).
  • Accessibility: Using Scratch and block-based programming to create an experience that is easy to access and understand.

In conclusion, NEXUS BETHA aims to bridge the gap between scientific knowledge and practical understanding by allowing children to experience the decisions behind space exploration. Our goal is simple: turn young learners into the engineers, problem-solvers, and astronauts of tomorrow.
